title: A shared malignant dependency that renewing normal tissues can spare

concept.text: The proposed innovation is the discovery of a biological function, molecular complex, or cell state that cancers across unrelated carcinoma types need to survive, but that essential normal renewing tissues can tolerate losing for the duration of treatment. An intervention against that dependency would need to eliminate malignant cells while preserving the functioning and recovery of tissues such as bone marrow and gut mucosa. This is a discovery goal; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate its completion.

The defining advance would be the combination of breadth and selectivity, rather than the use of any particular target class. MYC inhibition, synthetic lethality, and interference with telomere maintenance provide relevant approaches. Synthetic lethality exploits a vulnerability created by another molecular defect: PARP inhibition in BRCA-mutant cancers demonstrates that a cancer-associated context can permit selective treatment. ONC-04 asks whether a sufficiently strong dependency can be shared across much broader carcinoma populations.

significance.text: A major obstacle to selective cancer treatment is that malignant cells use biological machinery also needed by healthy cells. MYC illustrates the problem: its physiological activities participate in tissue regeneration, while cancers can depend on its activity. A broadly shared malignant dependency whose inhibition preserves normal renewal would create a treatment window across unrelated carcinomas, extending beyond the restricted molecular contexts already demonstrated by therapies such as PARP inhibitors. The revolutionary feature would be this breadth of selective eradication, not the first existence of any therapeutic window in oncology.

Conditional synthesis: if an intervention could inhibit that dependency sufficiently at tolerable exposures, its direct benefit would be selective tumor killing across the demonstrated cancer types. This could support systemic treatment of disease at multiple sites. Reliable eradication throughout the body would still require adequate distribution, sustained target inhibition, control of resistant populations, and acceptable toxicities beyond injury to renewing tissues. Target essentiality and normal-tissue dispensability alone would not guarantee a cure or a predictable overall safety margin.

The proposed breadth should not be confused with literal universality. Successful treatment of several unrelated carcinomas would be a substantial advance but would not establish efficacy against every carcinoma, every malignant cell state, or all cancers. Whether a dependency with the necessary breadth and selectivity exists remains uncertain. Metabolic manipulation, including a proposed shift toward oxidative phosphorylation, or telomere-maintenance inhibition would qualify only if it met the same selectivity, eradication, and durability requirements; naming a mechanism does not establish that capability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a pharmacologically actionable dependency that remains essential across unrelated carcinomas while normal renewing tissues tolerate its inhibition. Finding a vulnerability in one genotype or tissue context is insufficient to establish that breadth. The supplied synthetic-lethality review identifies cell and tissue specificity as an obstacle to translating interactions into broadly applicable treatments. A candidate dependency therefore needs evidence that its apparent selectivity persists across biological contexts rather than reflecting a narrow experimental setting.

Druggability and selectivity are separate engineering challenges. MYC's intrinsically disordered structure complicates traditional drug development, while its role in normal regeneration complicates the choice of exposure and treatment duration. The structural point applies specifically to MYC in the supplied evidence; it does not justify describing all transcription factors as disordered. A successful intervention must reach and inhibit its target strongly enough to eliminate tumors while allowing essential normal tissue functions to continue or recover.

Biological escape can undermine an apparently shared dependency. Telomere maintenance illustrates this complication: the supplied ALT review estimates that approximately 10–15% of cancers use alternative lengthening of telomeres, a telomerase-independent mechanism driven by homologous recombination. It also describes the ability to transition from telomerase-dependent states. Consequently, targeting telomerase alone cannot be assumed to cover all telomere-maintenance strategies or prevent adaptation.

Engineering synthesis: the discovery must connect causal dependence to achievable exposure, durable tumor elimination, and preserved tissue function. Early target engagement establishes that an intervention affects the intended biology; it does not establish that inhibition is deep or sustained enough for eradication. Resistance, inaccessible tumor sites, and toxicities outside renewing tissues remain additional barriers even if the core dependency is identified.

current_state.text: The MYC review published on 19 February 2025 reported that no MYC inhibitor had yet been approved for clinical use. This is a dated statement from the review's accessible abstract and subscription preview, not an independently established approval assessment for November 2026. The supplied research does not contain a later field-wide update.

The OMO-103 first-in-human phase 1 study, published on 6 February 2024, treated 22 patients with advanced solid tumors. Nineteen were evaluable for efficacy; 12 reached the scheduled 9-week assessment, and eight had stable disease as their best response. No objective response according to RECIST was reported. One patient classified as having stable disease had a 49% reduction in total measured tumor volume. That volumetric finding should be preserved alongside, rather than substituted for, the RECIST classification. The study supported tolerability and early target engagement, including biopsy transcriptional findings, but did not establish curative efficacy.

The same trial article describes prior genetic expression of Omomyc that prevented tumorigenesis and eradicated tumors in multiple cancer models, providing a preclinical basis for pursuing the broader goal. Those model results are distinct from treatment of patients with administered OMO-103. The supplied review retained the main article's HTML prose, which supports the clinical counts and conclusions above. Visual panels and linked supplements were not inspected; the PDF had extraction gaps, and the reporting-summary supplement was effectively unreadable in extraction. These limitations restrict supplementary assessment without negating the results documented in the main text.

A synthetic-lethality review published online on 11 September 2025, with a January 2026 issue date, identified PARP inhibition in BRCA-mutant cancers as clinical proof of concept and described limited clinical translation of other synthetic-lethal interactions. Its retained abstract also emphasized cell and tissue specificity. This establishes selective therapeutic benefit in a restricted molecular context, rather than a dependency that has been shown to eradicate unrelated carcinomas broadly. The review body was unavailable in the supplied evidence.

The November 2024 review of imetelstat reported US approval in June 2024 for a defined population of adults with lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes and transfusion-dependent anemia. It reported significantly greater red-cell transfusion independence than placebo, demonstrating a clinical benefit from telomerase inhibition. It also reported neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, so this achievement does not demonstrate complete sparing of normal marrow function. The retained PubMed abstract documents investigation in solid tumors and hematologic malignancies, but does not establish the earlier research assertion that a non-small-cell lung cancer trial failed. The full review was not supplied or inspected, and this abstract does not resolve the broader solid-tumor efficacy claim.

The ALT review published on 18 February 2025 estimated that approximately 10–15% of cancers use alternative lengthening of telomeres. This is an approximate proportion across cancers, not a stated prevalence for each carcinoma type. Its accessible abstract supports the telomerase-independent mechanism and potential switching between maintenance strategies; the full review body was behind a subscription preview.

Evidence-bound synthesis: the supplied dated reports establish restricted synthetic-lethal treatment, preclinical MYC-directed tumor eradication, early clinical MYC inhibition with disease control, and an approved telomerase inhibitor for a defined MDS population. They do not demonstrate the proposed broadly curative dependency. The supplied materials contain no completed freshness assessment establishing the field's full status on 1 November 2026; that gap does not invalidate the historical findings or establish that later advances have not occurred.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: one intervention directed at one defined dependency should produce durable tumor eradication across several unrelated carcinoma types at exposures that preserve marrow, gut mucosa, and other essential renewing tissues. The demonstration must state whether it concerns animal models or patients. Preclinical eradication would establish a model-based capability; it would not by itself establish a clinical cure. These are proposed criteria for ONC-04, not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: One intervention durably eradicates unrelated carcinomas while sparing renewing tissues

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal and durability requirements: experiments should establish that tumor elimination depends on inhibition of the intended target, define how eradication is measured, and specify the follow-up interval and relapse assessment. They should distinguish lasting elimination from temporary regression or disease control. Tissue assessment should measure function and recovery during and after treatment, rather than relying only on survival or the absence of gross injury. Activity in one genotype, stable disease in a phase 1 cohort, or target engagement alone would not satisfy this proposed breadth-and-eradication goal.
completion_criteria.label: Target-dependent lasting eradication accompanies measured normal-tissue function and recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: findings should reproduce in independent studies across multiple tumor backgrounds, with the tested cancer types, molecular contexts, exposures, schedules, and normal-tissue effects explicitly reported. A clinical claim should demonstrate benefit at exposures achievable in patients and assess toxicity, recurrence, and treatment feasibility. No numerical follow-up threshold is established by the supplied evidence. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth under specified conditions, not universal dependence across all cancers.
completion_criteria.label: Independent studies reproduce findings across tumor backgrounds under reported conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ONC-05, therapies that drive the whole clonal population to extinction, concerns eliminating every surviving and potentially resistant population. ONC-04 concerns the breadth and normal-tissue selectivity of the dependency being attacked. A broadly shared target could help achieve clonal extinction, but residual cells might escape it. ONC-07, body-wide delivery that alters essentially every malignant cell, addresses whether an intervention reaches and acts on cells throughout the body. Selective target biology does not itself solve that distribution problem.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-02, sterilizing immune clearance of established metastatic carcinomas, seeks eradication through immune action. ONC-12, off-the-shelf cell therapy that matches autologous cures and can be given at ordinary scale, adds a therapeutic platform and manufacturing-access goal. Either could overlap with ONC-04 if it exploits the proposed dependency, but immune clearance, scalable cell therapy, and broadly selective dependency inhibition remain distinct capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-03, eradication of dormant disseminated tumor cells that cause late relapse, focuses on a particular residual cell state. A dependency demonstrated in actively growing tumors would need separate testing in dormant cells before it could be assumed to solve ONC-03. ONC-06, stable reversion of carcinoma cells to non-malignant tissue identity, seeks durable normalization of cell behavior; ONC-04 instead proposes removing a malignant survival requirement to achieve tumor eradication. A cell-state mechanism could create overlap without making the goals interchangeable.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-01, mortality-reducing detection of lethal cancers while they are still localized, and ONC-10, a reliable distinction between early neoplasms that will kill and those that will not, concern finding and interpreting disease before treatment. ONC-11, real-time, cell-resolution guidance that makes incomplete cancer surgery uncommon, concerns local removal. A systemic dependency-directed treatment could complement these capabilities, including treatment of residual disease, but would not itself establish earlier detection, prognostic discrimination, or more complete surgery.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-08, interception of non-viral precancers before they invade, concerns progression prevention, while ONC-09, prophylactic immunity that prevents the common non-viral cancers, concerns preventing cancer through immunity. A vulnerability in established carcinomas cannot automatically be assumed to exist in precancers or to support prophylactic immunity. Preventive applications would also require their own exposure, safety, and benefit demonstrations.

change_log.change: Preserved ONC-04's identity while defining the advance as broad, selective dependency inhibition rather than a particular target or an achieved general cure.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports a coherent discovery goal and narrower achievements, without establishing completion.

change_log.change: Replaced the universal tumor-versus-host dose dilemma and the assertion that no therapeutic index exists with a conditional account of broader selective treatment.
change_log.reason: The PARP example already demonstrates therapeutic selectivity in a restricted molecular context; systemic eradication also depends on exposure, resistance, and other toxicities.

change_log.change: Limited the structural druggability claim to MYC and added biological context as a barrier.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports MYC's intrinsic disorder and synthetic lethality's cell and tissue specificity, not universal disorder of transcription factors.

change_log.change: Corrected OMO-103 efficacy reporting to distinguish 22 treated patients, 19 efficacy-evaluable patients, 12 reaching the scheduled assessment, and eight with stable disease.
change_log.reason: The earlier wording blurred denominators and used response terminology too loosely; no objective RECIST response was reported.

change_log.change: Retained the 49% tumor-volume reduction alongside its stable-disease RECIST classification and incorporated prior Omomyc model eradication.
change_log.reason: These are useful quantitative and preclinical findings, but neither establishes clinical curative activity.

change_log.change: Dated the MYC approval statement and distinguished online publication from issue date for the synthetic-lethality review.
change_log.reason: Historical statements remain informative without implying a verified field update through November 2026.

change_log.change: Qualified the imetelstat solid-tumor claims and added its reported neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.
change_log.reason: The retained abstract supports a restricted MDS approval, transfusion benefit, and solid-tumor investigation, but not the claimed NSCLC failure or complete marrow sparing.

change_log.change: Preserved the approximate 10–15% ALT estimate and integrated alternative maintenance and switching as barriers.
change_log.reason: The supplied abstract supports both the numerical estimate and a relevant escape mechanism, without establishing carcinoma-specific prevalence.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion demonstration to include causal dependence, experimental setting, durability, tissue function, reproducibility, and practical exposure.
change_log.reason: These additions make the proposal interpretable while distinguishing preclinical success, clinical cure, and finite demonstrated breadth.

change_log.change: Retained access and extraction limits and separated all roster concepts through explicit overlap explanations.
change_log.reason: The record should preserve the evidence's actual scope and related goals without implying inspection of unavailable material or merging distinct innovations.

unresolved_issues: Whether a dependency with the proposed breadth, durability, and normal-tissue selectivity exists remains unknown.
The supplied evidence does not establish the field's complete status or MYC inhibitor approval status on 1 November 2026.

The asserted failed non-small-cell lung cancer trial and the broader imetelstat solid-tumor cure claim remain unresolved by the retained abstract; lack of support here is not proof that either assertion is false.
The original mutant-p53 and chromosome-instability target survey is not substantiated by the supplied review and therefore is not presented as established evidence.
The proposed oxidative-phosphorylation route lacks supporting evidence in the supplied materials and is retained only as a conditional example.

The completion proposal still requires selection of a cancer panel, eradication measurements, follow-up duration, and quantitative tissue-function boundaries; the supplied evidence establishes no numerical consensus thresholds.

Review bodies available only as abstracts or subscription previews, along with uninspected OMO-103 panels and supplements, limit further assessment. The main HTML prose supports the retained OMO-103 results despite PDF extraction problems.

brief.title: A shared cancer weakness that healthy tissues can spare
possible: People with several unrelated types of cancer could receive a treatment that eliminates their tumors while preserving bone marrow and the gut lining. It would block a biological function those cancers need to survive, but that healthy tissues can tolerate losing during treatment.
why: Cancer cells rely on much of the same machinery as healthy cells. Finding a shared weakness that healthy tissues can spare would give patients across different cancer types a wider opportunity for selective treatment.
A treatment aimed at that weakness could attack cancer at multiple sites in the body. Its reach would extend beyond treatments whose selectivity depends on a particular genetic defect.

sources.who: Jonathan R. Whitfield and Laura Soucek
sources.showed: Their review describes efforts to block MYC, a protein that controls programs involved in cancer growth. Its lack of a fixed structure makes traditional drug development difficult.
sources.cited_for: MYC offers a possible shared target, but making an effective drug against it is difficult.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish lasting elimination of unrelated cancers while preserving healthy tissue renewal.

sources.who: Elena Garralda, Marie-Eve Beaulieu and colleagues
sources.showed: An early safety trial of the MYC blocker OMO-103 found tolerability and disease control. One patient's total tumor volume fell by 49%, but their response remained classified as stable disease. No response met the trial's standard criteria for tumor shrinkage.
sources.quote:
Transcriptomic analysis supported target engagement in 
tumor biopsies.
sources.cited_for: OMO-103 affected its intended biology in tumor samples and showed early clinical activity.
sources.not_established: The small trial did not demonstrate tumor eradication or lasting preservation of essential renewing tissues.

sources.who: Emanuel Gonçalves, Colm J. Ryan and David J. Adams
sources.showed: Their review describes synthetic lethality: exploiting a weakness caused by another molecular defect. It identifies successful treatment in selected genetic settings and explains why broader translation remains difficult.
sources.quote: Although the clinical success of PARP inhibition in BRCA-mutant cancers stands as proof of concept, few other synthetic lethal interactions have been translated from preclinical findings into effective therapies.
sources.cited_for: Selective treatment can exploit a cancer's genetic context, but these weaknesses often depend on cell and tissue type.
sources.not_established: Success in selected genetic settings does not establish a shared weakness across unrelated cancers.

sources.showed: Their review reports that imetelstat reduced transfusion dependence in a defined group with a bone marrow disorder. It blocks telomerase, an enzyme that maintains chromosome ends, but also caused low blood cell counts.
sources.quote: and imetelstat was associated with a manageable safety profile characterized primarily by short-lived and manageable neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.
sources.cited_for: Blocking telomerase can provide clinical benefit, while also harming blood cell production.
sources.not_established: This benefit does not establish broad elimination of solid cancers or complete sparing of normal marrow function.

sources.who: Apurwa Mishra and Trupti N. Patel
sources.showed: Their review describes how some cancers maintain chromosome ends without telomerase. It also discusses their ability to switch from relying on telomerase to this alternative route.
sources.cited_for: Alternative ways to maintain chromosome ends illustrate how cancers could escape a proposed shared weakness.
sources.not_established: Blocking telomerase alone does not establish coverage of alternative maintenance routes or prevent adaptation.

shown: Researchers using Omomyc, a tool that blocks MYC, eliminated tumors in multiple animal cancer models by making cells produce it genetically. This is the strongest tumor-elimination result described, but it differs from giving patients a drug.
Garralda and colleagues tested administered OMO-103 in 22 patients with advanced solid tumors. The early trial supported tolerability and disease control, but did not demonstrate eradication.
missing: A drug-accessible weakness must remain essential across unrelated cancer types while healthy renewing tissues tolerate its loss.
Treatment must reach tumors and block that weakness strongly and long enough to eliminate them.
Lasting tumor elimination must accompany measured marrow and gut function and recovery.
Independent studies must reproduce the results across different tumor backgrounds and assess resistance.

milestones.label: One treatment durably eliminates unrelated cancers while sparing renewing tissues
milestones.explanation: One treatment would have to eliminate several unrelated cancer types durably while preserving essential renewing tissues. Whether this occurs in animals or patients determines the strength of the claim.

milestones.label: Lasting elimination depends on the target, with tissue recovery measured
milestones.explanation: Experiments would have to link lasting elimination to blocking the intended target and measure healthy tissue function and recovery. This would distinguish selective eradication from temporary control.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce results across tumor backgrounds under stated conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce results across tumor backgrounds under stated treatment conditions. Clinical claims would also require achievable doses, acceptable toxicity and assessment of recurrence and feasibility.

uncertain: It remains unknown whether a weakness with the required breadth, lasting effect and healthy tissue selectivity exists.
The cancer types, follow-up duration and acceptable tissue-function limits needed to judge success remain unsettled.
Cancers may escape by switching biological routes or retaining resistant cell populations.

page.title: A cancer-selective dependency shared across carcinomas
page.definition: One biological function is required for survival by unrelated carcinoma types, cancers arising from epithelial cells, and can be inhibited to eliminate their tumors while essential renewing normal tissues continue functioning or recover after treatment. The demonstrated scope is the tested cancer populations.

goal.need: Worldwide cancer incidence in 2022 was about 20 million cases, with 9.7 million deaths; these totals include cancers outside this entry’s carcinoma scope. PARP inhibition in BRCA-mutant cancers establishes clinical proof of concept for selective dependency targeting. Its success does not establish a dependency shared across unrelated carcinomas: the synthetic-lethality review identifies cell and tissue specificity as a barrier to translation.

figures.caption: Estimated worldwide cancer burden in 2022
figures.note: All cancers; these figures do not estimate the population eligible for a shared-dependency treatment.

statements.body: Wellcome Sanger Institute, Cancer Dependency Map
statements.quote: aims to assign a dependency to every cancer cell in a patient, which could be exploited to develop new therapies.
statements.context: The programme seeks coverage through a map of vulnerabilities; it does not assert that one dependency is shared by every cancer.

statements.quote: with the goal of bringing a new therapeutic approach to patients with MYC-driven cancers.
statements.context: Development objective for the MYC inhibitor OMO-103, stated on 24 March 2026.

completion.title: Independent clinical studies confirm tumor clearance across carcinomas with preserved normal renewal.
completion.criterion: Independent clinical studies establish that inhibiting the same identified dependency produces complete remissions persisting after treatment stops across unrelated carcinoma histologies, while marrow blood-cell production and intestinal mucosal function continue or recover. Registered protocols must define disease-detection limits, recurrence surveillance, follow-up and tissue-function endpoints. The claim covers only the tested populations and observation periods. No external numerical threshold for the combined capability was found; RECIST complete response alone does not establish eradication.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; no external body was found to have specified this combined test.
completion.basis: Searched FDA tissue-agnostic oncology guidance, ICH S9, RECIST 1.1, MYCure trial endpoints, and Sanger and Peptomyc programme statements. None defines a joint test for shared dependence, off-treatment remission and normal renewal. This qualitative fallback combines their therapeutic goals with independent clinical confirmation; numerical boundaries require protocol-specific definitions.

milestones.title: A candidate inhibits tumors in preclinical models with its mechanism and dosing schedule characterized.
milestones.criterion: Before human testing, a candidate demonstrates antitumor activity, with preliminary characterization of mechanism and schedule dependence, as recommended by ICH S9; no universal regression percentage is specified. Published example: Beaulieu and colleagues’ 2019 study reported reduced growth of H1975 human lung-cancer xenografts with intravenous Omomyc, 60 mg/kg four times weekly, with 14 mice per group. This demonstrated growth inhibition rather than eradication.
milestones.set_by: ICH S9, section 2.1, adopted by FDA in March 2010; nonbinding recommendations for anticancer pharmaceuticals.
milestones.threshold_quote: preliminary characterization of the mechanism(s) of action and schedule dependencies, as well as anti-tumor activity of the pharmaceutical, should have been made.

milestones.title: A first-in-human trial establishes a dose for further testing and shows tumor target engagement.
milestones.criterion: The MYCure protocol selects a recommended phase 2 dose using safety, antitumor activity, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Dose-limiting toxicity is a possibly drug-related grade ≥3 event within 21 days. The report published on 6 February 2024 treated 22 patients with OMO-103; 6.48 mg/kg weekly was selected, with transcriptional evidence of tumor target engagement. The safety committee also counted one grade 2 pancreatitis as dose-limiting. This establishes neither normal-tissue sparing nor tumor eradication.
milestones.set_by: Peptomyc and the MYCure investigators, registered study NCT04808362 and its published Methods; this protocol concerns OMO-103 in advanced solid tumors.
milestones.threshold_quote: RP2D was selected based on clinical safety/tolerability, antitumor activity, PK and PD data.

milestones.title: A dependency-directed drug produces a RECIST 1.1 complete response in a patient with carcinoma.
milestones.criterion: RECIST 1.1 overall complete response requires disappearance of target and non-target lesions, pathological lymph nodes reduced to <10 mm short axis, normalization of applicable tumor markers and no new lesions. Nonrandomized trials with response as the primary endpoint require confirmation at a subsequent protocol-specified assessment. In MYCure, 19 patients were response-evaluable; none had an objective response. Eight of 12 reaching 9 weeks had stable disease; one patient with stable disease had a 49% total tumor-volume reduction. Complete response establishes detectable disease clearance, not cure.
milestones.set_by: RECIST Working Group, revised RECIST guideline version 1.1, sections 4.3–4.6.
milestones.threshold_quote: Complete Response (CR): Disappearance of all target lesions.

milestones.title: One clinical study shows off-treatment tumor clearance across carcinomas with preserved normal renewal.
milestones.criterion: One prospective study demonstrates complete remissions persisting off treatment in unrelated carcinoma histologies through inhibition of the same dependency, while marrow and intestinal function meet its prespecified preservation or recovery endpoints. Histology coverage, follow-up and acceptable tissue-function changes must be defined in the registered protocol. This is the initial joint clinical demonstration before independent confirmation; no published result meeting it was located.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; searches of FDA guidance, RECIST and dependency-development programmes found no published joint milestone or numerical boundary.

not_found: No externally specified carcinoma panel, remission duration, response fraction or marrow and gut preservation limits were found for the combined capability.
The ClinicalTrials.gov page for NCT04808362 did not expose its protocol fields; the published trial Methods supplied the endpoints.

results.finding: In 22 patients, OMO-103’s recommended phase 2 dose was 6.48 mg/kg weekly.
results.detail: Dose selection considered safety, preliminary activity, pharmacokinetics, target engagement and biomarkers. Paired biopsies provided transcriptional evidence of target engagement. One grade 2 pancreatitis was counted as dose-limiting.
results.quote:
Based on all these 
data, the recommended phase 2 dose was determined as DL5 (6.48 mg kg−1).

results.finding: Among 19 response-evaluable patients receiving OMO-103, none had an objective RECIST response.
results.detail: No complete response was reported. One patient with stable disease had a 49% reduction in total tumor volume.
results.quote:
even though there was no 
objective response to treatment according to RECIST criteria

results.finding: Omomyc reduced growth of H1975 lung-cancer xenografts in 14 mice per group at 60 mg/kg.
results.detail: Intravenous treatment was given four times weekly. The study also characterized MYC inhibition and tested other doses and schedules; the reported result was growth inhibition, not eradication.

results.finding: MYCi975 inhibited MycCaP tumor growth in 6–7 grafts per group, from 4 mice per group.
results.detail: Daily dosing was 100 mg/kg for 14 days; an intermittent schedule also slowed growth. The study characterized MYC binding, disruption of MYC/MAX interaction, and increased MYC degradation.

results.finding: Larotrectinib produced complete responses in 3 of 24 patients with TRK fusion differentiated thyroid carcinoma.
results.detail: Responses were assessed by independent review under RECIST 1.1 and confirmed at least 4 weeks after the initial response.
results.quote: ORR was 79% (95% confidence interval (CI): 58–93); best responses were complete response in 3 (13%) patients, partial response in 16 (67%), stable disease in 3 (13%), progressive disease in 1 (4%) and not evaluable in 1 (4%).

results.finding: Among 4 patients with RET fusion–positive pancreatic cancer, 1 had a confirmed complete response to pralsetinib.
results.detail: The efficacy-evaluable population included 23 patients. Responses were assessed by blinded independent central review using RECIST 1.1.
results.quote: Confirmed tumor responses were observed in all four patients with pancreatic cancer (including one CR), two of three patients with cholangiocarcinoma, two of three patients with sarcoma (including one CR), two of three patients with neuroendocrine cancer and single patients with head and neck cancer and unknown primary tumor (CR).

results.finding: In 41 efficacy-evaluable patients treated with selpercatinib, one patient with breast cancer had a complete response.
results.detail: Responses were assessed using RECIST 1.1 and required central confirmation more than four weeks after the initial assessment. The breast cancer patient had no measurable disease.
results.quote: One additional patient with breast cancer had no measurable disease (not shown on the plot) and was determined to have a complete response.

results.finding: In ROAR, 3 of 36 patients with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma had an investigator-assessed complete response.
results.detail: Responses were assessed using RECIST 1.1, but the provided text does not establish confirmation at a subsequent protocol-specified assessment, as required for this single-arm trial.

results.finding: Among 24 patients with TRK fusion thyroid carcinoma, 3 had a complete response.
results.detail: All three discontinued study treatment and were alive without progression at their last evaluable assessment. The analysis covers thyroid carcinoma only; it does not establish persistent off-treatment remission or prespecified marrow and intestinal preservation or recovery.
results.quote: All three patients with a CR had discontinued treatment and were alive without disease progression at their last evaluable tumour assessment.

results.finding: Pralsetinib produced confirmed complete responses in 3 of 23 efficacy-evaluable patients with RET fusion–positive solid tumors.
results.detail: The responses included pancreatic cancer, sarcoma and an unknown primary. The study does not establish complete remission off treatment across unrelated carcinomas or prespecified marrow and intestinal preservation or recovery.

results.finding: Selpercatinib produced complete responses in 2 of 41 patients with RET fusion-positive solid tumours.
results.detail: The study reports responses across tumour types, but does not establish complete remissions persisting off treatment across unrelated carcinomas or prespecified marrow and intestinal preservation or recovery.
results.quote: a complete response was attained in two (5%) of 41 patients

results.finding: In 36 patients with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, 3 had a complete response by investigator assessment.
results.detail: The phase 2 study also reported responses in other carcinoma cohorts. It does not establish complete remissions persisting off treatment across unrelated carcinoma histologies or prespecified marrow and intestinal preservation or recovery endpoints.

results.finding: HRO761 achieved approximately 70% disease control across MSI xenograft models, with 5–7 mice per model.

results.finding: Among 27 patients with TRK fusion salivary gland cancer, 9 had complete responses to larotrectinib.
results.detail: Responses were assessed by independent review using RECIST 1.1. The abstract does not identify the tumors as carcinomas or state whether complete responses were confirmed at a subsequent assessment.
results.quote: The overall response rate (ORR) was 85% (95% confidence interval [CI] 66–96), including 9 (33%) complete responses, 14 (52%) partial responses, 2 (7%) stable disease, and 2 (7%) progressive disease.
